hints: Notice the train is a receding source at $50 \text{m s}^{-1}$ while the man is stationary, so each wavefront is emitted further back and the observed wavelength is stretched.
Recall the Doppler shift for a receding source: observed wavelength $\lambda' = (v+v_s)/f_0$ and observed frequency $f' = v/\lambda'$.
Calculate the new $f'$ from $400 \text{Hz}$, $340 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $50 \text{m s}^{-1}$, then subtract it from $400 \text{Hz}$ to get the difference.
walkthrough: First case gives the source frequency: with the train stationary the man hears $f_0 = 400 \text{Hz}$.
For the receding train, use speed of sound $v = 340 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and source speed $v_s = 50 \text{m s}^{-1}$. The observed wavelength is stretched to $\lambda' = (v + v_s)/f_0$.
Hence observed frequency is $f' = v/\lambda' = f_0 \times v/(v+v_s) = 400 \times 340/(340+50)$.
Substitute: $f' = 400 \times 340/390 \approx 348.7 \text{Hz}$, about $349 \text{Hz}$ with correct units of $\text{Hz}$.
The question asks for the difference: $\Delta f = f_0 - f' \approx 400 - 348.7 \approx 51.3 \text{Hz}$, about $51 \text{Hz}$.

options.A: Observed frequency is about $349 \text{Hz}$, so the drop from $400 \text{Hz}$ is about $51 \text{Hz}$.
options.B: About $69 \text{Hz}$ would result from using $50 \text{m s}^{-1}$ incorrectly in the numerator instead of in the stretched wavelength.
options.C: $349 \text{Hz}$ is the new observed frequency for the receding train, not the difference from $400 \text{Hz}$.
options.D: $469 \text{Hz}$ would be an increased frequency for an approaching source, not a receding source moving away.
